title: Pakistan will come to be
takeaway: When a people unite with courage and faith, nothing can stop them.
scene: 'Ban ke rahe ga Pakistan', 'Pakistan will come to be', was a famous slogan of the 1940s independence movement. This poem is written like a marching song, with that line repeated as a chorus. It imagines the days before 1947, when people were fighting for the new country.
context: A poem of its time. It was written at a particular moment in Pakistan's history and uses the political language of that moment. It is translated faithfully so you can see how people spoke then. Translating it is not the same as agreeing with every line. It was sung in the 1940s, during the campaign for Pakistan. The harsh words for opponents belong to that struggle.

couplets.story: The chorus: Pakistan is our honour and our pride, and it will happen!

translation: Hundreds of thousands of opponents make a racket,
couplets.story: Huge numbers of opponents are shouting that India should never be divided.
But the Muslims have woken up. Pakistan is going to happen.

original: کھل کے واہ پے لان فرنگی
ہند و سکھ تے لو نا نگی
transliteration: Khul ke vaah pe laan Farangi
Hindu Sikh te lo naa nangi
translation: The British are trying everything they can,
and the Hindus and Sikhs too.
couplets.story: The British and other groups are doing all they can to stop it.

original: اوڑک نوں سب موہنہ دی کھان
transliteration: Orak nu sab moonh di khaan
translation: In the end they'll all fall flat on their faces:
couplets.story: In the end, all their efforts will fail. Pakistan will happen.

translation: A clear word has come from the Qur'an;
the command of the Merciful Lord has come.
couplets.story: The poet feels God's promise is on their side.
They will win. Pakistan will happen.

original: کفر دے اگے سینہ تن کے
transliteration: Kufr de agge seena tan ke
translation: Becoming like Tariq, Khalid and Haider,
couplets.story: People are being as brave as the great Muslim heroes of history, Tariq, Khalid and Ali, standing up tall against their opponents.

translation: they've come out onto the field:
couplets.story: They've stepped out into the open, ready. Pakistan will happen.

translation: who woke up the sleeping nation,
couplets.story: They are Jinnah's fearless followers, and he woke up a sleeping people.
Jinnah is their strong leader. Pakistan will happen.

translation: The Muslims have woken up now,
and their opponents are losing the game.
couplets.story: The Muslims have woken up, and the other side is losing.
The poet ends by saying Pakistan is a gift from God, and it will happen.

deeper: This is a 1940s political song, and it should be read as history. It uses faith as a source of courage: 'a clear word has come from the Qur'an' and 'it is God's gift'. The deeper idea is trust (tawakkul): people do their part and believe God is with them. Its lines about Hindus, Sikhs and the British reflect the struggle of that time.
why: It captures the spirit of the 1940s independence movement as people at the time felt it, using one of its most famous slogans.
prompt: What's something people once said 'will never happen' that did happen, because people believed in it?
notes: Printed in two columns of short lines with the refrain; the reading order is approximate.
Uses strong 1940s political language ('kufr', 'kaafir') for opponents of Pakistan. The app should present this as historical context.
